## Question 1 (40-points)

Please watch the following video on data visualization [here](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jbkSRLYSojo&t=121s) .

After you have watched the entire video, please answer the following questions.

The data used in the video are pre-loaded into R, and called `gapminder`. You are going to both re-create a still image, and the animated version of his plot. Here are some things to consider:


The x-axis uses a logarithmic scale in the video. At the beginning, around 0:30, he introduces income values of \$400, \$4,000, and $40,000. Those values are equally spaced on the graph even though each is ten times the previous value. We can transform our x-axis to be on a logarithmic scale by using the function `scale_x_log10()` with no other arguments. 

To hide the legends, as seen in the video, please see the help file for `theme()` and search the `legend.position = ` argument.

a. Pause the video when Hans Rosling is showing data for the year 1977. Screenshot this image, and embed this into your quarto document. Note: put this image in an images folder in your repo, write the correct file path to embed the picture. 

Underneath the picture, define the following: 

-- x-axis 

-- y-axis 

-- size of the dots 

In addition, define the number of regions Hans is showing, and share the color that each represent.

b. In the `gapminder` data set, there are 5 total regions in the `continent` column. Our goal is to match the Hans plot as best as possible. To do this, we need to combine `Oceania` and `Asia` together. 

      > Create a new variable called region that changes "Oceania" to "Asia", using if_else(). Save and overwrite the existing gapminder data set.
      > Create and show a contingency table of the variable region to show that there are only 4 unique regions in your data set.


::: {.cell}

:::



c. In the same code chunk... 

-- create a new dataset called gapminder1977 that only has data for the year 1977.
      
-- use these data to recreate the plot you pasted in part a. 

      > You do not need to have the large Year value in your plot. Instead, put this in your title
      > The axes do not need to have the same font, and can be the generic axes labels outside of the plot       > You do not need "years" under the y-axis labels.
      
      
      > The colors must match. You may reference the generic color names when setting the colors.
      > The y-axis must show the values 25, 50, and 70. We can do this by setting arguments in scale_y_continuous(). Please see the arguments breaks = and limits =.
      > Your x-axis should show 400, 4,000, and 40,000. You can set this in the scale_x_log10() function using the breaks = argument. 
      > Your x-axis should have $ before 400, 4,000, and 40,000. You can set this using the labels argument in the scale_x-log10() function. Note: label_dollar() is in the scales package. Directly call the label_dollar() function from the scales package. Do not library scales for this assignment. 




::: {.cell}

:::




d.  You will give many presentations as a statistician/data scientist/researcher. Communicating data to a general audience is one of the most important skills one can develop. Reflecting on the video, please answer the following questions.

      > What is one way that Hans Rosling was effective in communicating the story of the data?

      > What is one strategy you may try and implement during a future presented? 

## Question 2 (10-points)

Now, we are going to re-create his animation! Please note that when you render to a PDF, your plot will not animate. Animation only works on non-static documents like a HTML document. 

To do this, we are going to...

      > Copy your code from question-1 part c into a new code chunk here. Save your plot as a R object, p. 
      > use the function transition_time() with the argument of your time variable you want your plot to animate through. 
      > Make sure you are using the entire data set, and not the filtered data set 
      > Update the title of your plot to be "Year: {frame_time}". This creates a dynamic title where frame_time is updated according to the transition_time() variable.
      > This will not be supported as a pdf. Make sure to set your code chunk to echo: true and eval: false so we can still see your code. You should be able to see / enjoy your animation in the Viewer pane!


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
p <- ggplot(
  gapminder,
  aes(
    x = gdpPercap,
    y = lifeExp,
    size = pop,
    color = region
  )
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_x_log10(
  breaks = c(400, 4000, 40000),
  labels = scales::label_dollar()
) +
  scale_y_continuous(
  breaks = c(25, 50, 75),
  limits = c(25, NA)
) +
  labs(
    title = "Year: {frame_time}",
    x = "GDP per capita",
    y = "Life expectancy",
    size = "Population",
    color = "Region"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() + 
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
 scale_color_manual(
  values = c(
    "Americas" = "green",
    "Europe" = "yellow",
    "Africa" = "blue",
    "Asia" = "red"
  )
) +
  transition_time(year) 

animate(p, fps = 10, duration = 10)
```
